title: A Stinky Surprise: 800-Year-Old Latrine Yields a Wax Notebook and Silk Toilet Paper
summary: You might think an 800-year-old toilet would hold nothing but, well, ancient waste. But for archaeologists in Paderborn, Germany, a medieval latrine turned out to be a treasure chest. During construction near the Abdinghof monastery, workers uncovered five latrines from the 13th or 14th century. Inside one, nestled in a wet lump of earth, was a remarkably preserved notebook — and yes, it still carried what restorer Susanne Bretzel politely called an “unpleasant smell.” The notebook is a palm-sized marvel: about 3.4 by 2.2 inches, with 10 wax-coated pages bound in a wooden frame. Its owner used a stylus — a pointed tool of metal, ivory, or bone — to scratch notes in cursive Latin. The writing is a puzzle; the author wrote in multiple directions and sometimes overwrote previous words, making it “difficult to read at first glance,” said archaeologist Barbara Ruschoff-Parzinger. But after careful restoration, experts plan to use high-tech imaging to decipher the text. Who dropped this book? Sveva Gai, Paderborn’s city archaeologist, suspects a local merchant. “A Paderborn merchant may have been the author, jotting down business transactions and recording his thoughts,” she said. In an era when few could read, merchants were educated, and the use of Latin points to an upper-class individual. The leather case, embossed with fleur-de-lis patterns — a symbol of purity and royal power — reinforces that theory. The latrine held more clues to high-status life: scraps of fine silk, torn into rectangles. “Perhaps this was toilet paper, after the once noble fabric was to be thrown away,” Bretzel said. Alongside the silk were barrels, pottery, baskets, and a knife, all helping date the find. The notebook may have slipped from the merchant’s belt while he was, ahem, otherwise occupied. For archaeologists, latrines are “almost always a treasure pit,” Ruschoff-Parzinger noted, because organic materials survive in the damp, oxygen-poor conditions. This little book, once cleaned and scanned, could open a window onto daily life, trade, and even personal thoughts in medieval Westphalia. Not bad for a stinky old toilet.
why_it_matters: This find shows how even humble places like old toilets can preserve clues about ordinary life centuries ago, helping us understand trade, education, and personal habits in the Middle Ages. It reminds students that history isn't just about battles and kings—it's also about what people wrote, wore, and even used as toilet paper.

background_read: The city of Paderborn in western Germany was founded in the 8th century and was an important religious and trade center during the Middle Ages.
The Abdinghof monastery (a Benedictine monastery founded in 1015) was a place of learning and manuscript production, located in the city center.

In medieval times, latrines were often deep pits that, when abandoned, became sealed with layers of soil and waste, creating oxygen-poor conditions that preserve organic materials like wood, leather, and textiles.
Wax tablets like this one were common reusable writing surfaces in antiquity and the Middle Ages, used by merchants to keep accounts before paper became widely available.
The fleur-de-lis symbol (a stylized lily associated with French royalty) was often used on high-status items to suggest purity and power.

perspectives.description: The discovery provides a rare glimpse into medieval daily life, especially literacy and commerce among merchants. The notebook and silk scraps are physical touchpoints to a time when writing was a skill reserved for the few.

Such finds are initially repellent and require careful, messy cleaning before they become valuable artifacts. Not everyone would want to handle an 800-year-old toilet lump, but the results are worth it.

Because organic materials survive in waterlogged layers, latrines often yield objects that would never be preserved elsewhere. Archaeologists treat ancient toilets as time capsules that hold everyday items untouched by air.

High-tech imaging might reveal the merchant's notes, potentially shedding light on trade networks, language use, or personal reflections from the 13th century. If the text can be deciphered, it could open a new window onto medieval Westphalia.
